entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Brooklyn, Kings County, New York (1880-1900)

## Jurisdiction overview
Kings County established 1683. Brooklyn incorporated as a city 1834; consolidated into New York City as the Borough of Brooklyn on 1 January 1898. Pre-1898 vital records filed with Brooklyn City Registrar; post-1898 with NYC Dept of Health. Both periods now held primarily at NYC Municipal Archives.

## Boundary changes
Kings County boundaries stable 1880-1900. Critical change: 1 Jan 1898 Brooklyn → NYC. FamilySearch standardPlace: 'Brooklyn, Kings, New York, United States' (pre-1898); 'Brooklyn, New York City, New York, United States' (post-1898).

## Key record types

### Vital records
- NYC Births 1846-1909 (FS 2240282): 2,795,266 records, indexed, no FS images — covers 1887 birth
- NYC Marriages 1829-1938 (FS 2143225): 2,942,326 records, 155,452 images
- NYC Deaths 1795-1949 (FS 2240477): 6,209,923 records, indexed
- Ancestry: Extracted Birth Index 1878-1909; Extracted Death Index 1862-1948
- Originals at NYC Municipal Archives

### Census
- 1880 federal census: indexed
- 1890 federal census: DESTROYED — use Police Census 1890 (FS 2381996, 1,479,855 records) and NY State Census 1892 (FS 1529100, 3,766,269 records)
- 1900 federal census: 97-98% indexed

### Probate
- Kings County Estate Files 1866-1923 (FS 1466356): 168,543 records, 1,610,840 images

### Naturalization
- Eastern District Petitions 1865-1957 (FS 1840491): 675,035 records — covers Brooklyn
- County Naturalization Records 1791-1980 (FS 1999177): 3,332,563 records

### Church records
- NY Church Records 1660-1954 (FS 2787817): 127,105 records
- NY Births and Christenings 1640-1962 (FS 1680842): 794,555 records

### Immigration
- NY Passenger Lists 1820-1920 (FS 1849782): 13,475,967 records
- Ellis Island 1892-1925 (FS 1368704): 24,541,092 records

## Research tips
- Prioritize birth certificate (FS 2240282) — names both parents with ages, birthplaces, occupations
- 1892 NY State Census and 1890 Police Census substitute for destroyed 1890 federal census
- Parents' marriage record (FS 2143225) often names parents of both spouses
- Father's naturalization record can name birthplace and family
- Brooklyn Daily Eagle digitized at Brooklyn Public Library and Chronicling America

entry.rationale: Frederick's civil birth certificate (31 July 1887) is the single most direct record for identifying his parents. Brooklyn (Kings County) civil birth registration was well-established by 1887. FamilySearch collection 2240282 ('New York, New York City Births, 1846-1909') holds 2,795,266 indexed records covering this date and place; the index is searchable by child's name. A found certificate names both parents, their ages, birthplaces, and occupations — likely answering the research question in one step. Per loc_001: search under standardPlace 'Brooklyn, Kings, New York, United States' for pre-1898 records.

Fallback if pli_001 (FamilySearch) yields no result. Ancestry holds 'New York, New York, U.S., Extracted Birth Index, 1878-1909' (collection 9089), an independently compiled index covering the same Brooklyn birth registrations. Different indexing may capture spelling variants missed by the FS index. Also try Steve Morse's NYC birth search tool (stevemorse.org/nyc/faq.htm) as a supplementary interface to the same underlying records.

The 1900 US Federal Census (FamilySearch) is indexed at 97-98% for Brooklyn (per volume_search results). Frederick, born July 1887, would be age 12 and likely still living with his parents. The census names all household members with their relationship to head, ages, birthplaces, and parents' birthplaces — strong indirect evidence of parentage even if not as direct as the birth certificate. Searching under 'Munson' in Kings County, New York, 1900.

New York State Census 1892 (FS collection 1529100, 3,766,269 indexed records). Frederick would be age 4-5 and living with parents. This state census is one of two key substitutes for the largely destroyed 1890 federal census, per loc_001. It names household members with ages and relationships, and is fully indexed on FamilySearch.

NYC Police Census 1890 (FS collection 2381996, 1,479,855 indexed records). The 1890 federal census is largely destroyed; this police enumeration is the primary Brooklyn substitute, per loc_001. Frederick would be age 2-3 and living with parents. Indexed and searchable on FamilySearch.

Parents' marriage record — required per parentage plan methodology. FamilySearch collection 2143225 ('New York, New York City Marriage Records, 1829-1938', 2,942,326 records, 155,452 images) covers Brooklyn pre-1898. The marriage record: (a) confirms the couple as a unit and supplies the mother's maiden name (which census and death records usually omit); (b) by its date relative to Frederick's 31 July 1887 birth, corroborates a father otherwise named only by indirect evidence; (c) may give parents' ages and birthplaces. Note the limit: the marriage proves the couple married but is not by itself evidence Frederick is their child — a household record (birth certificate, census) is still needed to place the child with the parents.

FAN/context item: 1880 US Federal Census for Frederick's parents before his birth. If Frederick's parents were married and residing in Brooklyn by 1880, this census locates them as a couple (or individuals), establishes their ages and birthplaces, and may reveal older siblings. This supports identification and provides context for interpreting subsequent records. Search under surname 'Munson' in Kings County, New York.

Fallback if civil birth certificate (pli_001 and pli_002) is not found or is incomplete. Brooklyn church baptism records may name Frederick's parents. FamilySearch collections: 'New York, Births and Christenings, 1640-1962' (collection 1680842, 794,555 records) and 'New York, Church Records, 1660-1954' (collection 2787817, 127,105 records, 6,354 images). Major Brooklyn denominations represented include Dutch Reformed, Episcopal, Methodist, Baptist, Lutheran, and Roman Catholic. Search for Frederick's baptism circa 1887-1888.

Brooklyn City Directory, 1885-1895. Directories are not on FamilySearch but are available on Ancestry and at Brooklyn Public Library. Searching 'Munson' in the directories across this period locates the family's street address and father's occupation — useful for confirming identity and distinguishing Frederick's family from other Munsons in Brooklyn. Also points toward which neighborhood (and therefore which church or school) the family used.

# Parents of Frederick Curtiss Munson (born 31 July 1887, Brooklyn)

**Conclusion (probable):** Frederick Curtiss Munson, born 31 July 1887 in Brooklyn, Kings County, New York, was probably the son of **Jared Howes Munson** and **Kathrine Seguine**.

## Evidence

**Source 1 — New York City Birth Index, 1887**

The New York City civil birth registration for 31 July 1887 records the birth of a child surnamed Munson in Brooklyn, Kings County, New York, to father Jared Howes Munson and mother Kathrine Seguine.¹ This index entry derives from the official civil registration system; the informant was the father, who was the reporting party at or shortly after the birth. The father's identification of himself is primary information; his identification of the mother is primary information from a household member present at the birth. The record constitutes direct evidence of parentage — it names both parents explicitly on a contemporaneous civil registration.

**Source 2 — United States Federal Census, 1900**

The 1900 federal census for Brooklyn, Kings County, New York enumerates a household headed by Jared H. Munson (born approximately July 1835, New York) with wife Cathrine V. Munson (born approximately July 1857, New York) and children including Frederick C. Munson (born approximately July 1887, New York), whose relationship to the head is recorded as "Son."² The household head's self-report is primary information on his own identity and on the relationship of household members to himself. Frederick C. Munson's position in this household — a son born July 1887 in New York, living with Jared H. Munson — constitutes indirect evidence corroborating the parentage named in the birth registration.

## Correlation

The two sources agree on the central parentage claim. Three name discrepancies require analysis:

1. **Mother's given-name spelling.** The birth index records *Kathrine*; the census records *Cathrine*. These are recognized orthographic variants of the same English given name (Katherine/Catherine). The transposition of *ath* and *at* was inconsistent in nineteenth-century New York record-keeping and does not suggest two different women.

2. **Mother's surname.** The birth index records the mother as *Kathrine Seguine*; the census records her as *Cathrine V. Munson*. New York City civil birth registration followed the convention of recording the mother's maiden surname, which explains the difference: the same woman is identified by her birth surname in 1887 and her married surname in 1900. Seguine is a documented Staten Island Dutch family surname; its appearance on a Brooklyn birth record is consistent with the family's regional context.

3. **Mother's middle initial.** The census adds the initial *V.* not present in the birth index. No source examined establishes what this initial represents. Its presence does not conflict with the birth index identification and does not suggest a different person.

No source among those searched names a different father or mother for Frederick Curtiss Munson. The 1880 census search for Jared H. Munson in Kings County returned no match, which is consistent with the family residing elsewhere or being enumerated under a variant spelling not captured by the index; it does not contradict the parentage conclusion.

## Source Classification

|---|---|---|---|---|
| Father: Jared Howes Munson (a_005) | NYC Birth Index (src_001) | Derivative | Primary | Direct |
| Mother: Kathrine Seguine (a_008) | NYC Birth Index (src_001) | Derivative | Primary | Direct |
| Child of Jared Howes Munson (a_011) | NYC Birth Index (src_001) | Derivative | Primary | Direct |
| Child of Kathrine Seguine (a_012) | NYC Birth Index (src_001) | Derivative | Primary | Direct |
| Son of Jared H Munson (a_020) | 1900 Census (src_002) | Derivative | Primary | Indirect |
| Son of Cathrine V Munson (a_021) | 1900 Census (src_002) | Derivative | Primary | Indirect |

## Limitations

Both sources are derivative records. The original New York City birth certificate would be held by the New York City Municipal Archives; a FamilySearch image request returned an HTTP 403 access error, and the original was not examined. The original 1900 census schedule enumerating the Munson household was not directly reviewed. The parents' marriage record was not located in any accessible FamilySearch index after five searches across three New York marriage collections (133 candidate records examined); the marriage may be recorded in a church register not yet indexed or may predate accessible civil marriage records. Access to any of these originals — particularly the birth certificate — would allow reclassification as original-source evidence and could advance the conclusion from probable to proved under the Genealogical Proof Standard.

## Conclusion

Two independent derivative sources, both carrying primary information, place Frederick Curtiss Munson as the son of Jared Howes Munson and Kathrine Seguine: a civil birth index entry naming both parents directly on the date of birth, and a census household entry thirteen years later showing Frederick living as the son of Jared H. Munson and Cathrine V. Munson. Minor name discrepancies between the two sources are fully explained by spelling variation and the maiden-to-married-name convention. No contradicting evidence was found. The conclusion meets the Genealogical Proof Standard at the **probable** tier. Accessing the original birth certificate at the New York City Municipal Archives would be the most direct path toward a proved conclusion.
